This perspective fails to recognize the dynamic nature of human values, which evolve through interactions with technology and society. We introduce the Co-Evolutionary Value Alignment (CEVA) framework, which models the reciprocal relationship between evolving human values and developing AI capabilities. We present a formal model for representing value evolution, adaptive AI architectures that respond to value shifts while maintaining alignment with core safety principles, and bidirectional feedback mechanisms for transparent communication about value changes. Through extensive experimentation across gradual drift, rapid shift, and value conflict scenarios, we compare CEVA with traditional alignment approaches. Results indicate that adaptive alignment models significantly outperform static alignment methods in adaptation accuracy and user satisfaction, while maintaining reasonable stability. Our findings suggest that co-evolutionary approaches provide a promising direction for sustainable long-term alignment between humans and AI systems in dynamically evolving value landscapes.\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n## 1. Introduction\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\nThe rapid advancement of artificial intelligence has increasingly integrated AI systems into various aspects of human life, from personal assistants to healthcare, education, and governance. This integration has highlighted the critical importance of aligning AI systems with human values, preferences, and ethical standards. However, the prevailing approach to AI alignment has predominantly focused on a unidirectional process: adapting AI systems to conform to human values that are often treated as static, universal, and unambiguous targets.\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\nThis established paradigm fails to acknowledge a fundamental reality: human values are neither static nor monolithic. They evolve continuously in response to societal changes, technological advancements, cultural shifts, and interactions with the very AI systems we are attempting to align. The emergence of powerful AI technologies is itself a catalyst for value evolution, creating a complex feedback loop that current alignment frameworks do not adequately address.\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\nThe concept of bidirectional human-AI alignment has recently emerged as a response to these limitations. This approach recognizes that alignment is a dynamic, complex, and evolving process that involves both aligning AI with humans and facilitating human adaptation to AI systems. However, even within this bidirectional framework, there remains a critical gap in understanding and modeling the co-evolutionary dynamics of human values and AI capabilities.\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\nRecent work by Shen (2024) introduced a conceptual framework of \\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\"Bidirectional Human-AI Alignment\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\" through a systematic review of over 400 papers, encompassing both aligning AI to humans and aligning humans to AI. Similarly, Pedreschi et al. (2023) defined human-AI coevolution as a continuous mutual influence between humans and AI algorithms, emphasizing the complex feedback loops in human-AI interactions. The \\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\"Human-AI Handshake Model\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\" by Pyae (2025) further emphasizes a bidirectional, adaptive framework for human-AI collaboration with five key attributes: information exchange, mutual learning, validation, feedback, and mutual capability augmentation.\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\nBuilding on these foundations, this paper introduces the \\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\"Co-Evolutionary Value Alignment\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\" (CEVA) framework, a novel approach that explicitly models and facilitates the reciprocal relationship between evolving human values and developing AI capabilities. Unlike previous approaches that primarily focus on either aligning AI to current human values or helping humans adapt to AI systems, CEVA acknowledges that sustainable alignment requires understanding and shaping the trajectory of mutual adaptation between humans and AI over time.\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\nThe key contributions of this paper are:\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n1. A formal mathematical framework for modeling value evolution during human-AI interaction\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n2. An adaptive AI architecture that detects and responds to shifts in human values while maintaining alignment with core safety principles\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n3. Bidirectional feedback mechanisms for transparent communication about value changes\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n4. Empirical evaluation of the CEVA framework against baseline alignment approaches across various scenarios\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\nThe significance of this research lies in its potential to address a fundamental limitation in current alignment approaches. Without accounting for value co-evolution, even well-aligned AI systems may gradually drift out of alignment as human values shift in response to technological and social changes. By developing frameworks for sustainable long-term alignment, this research contributes to creating AI systems that can grow with humanity rather than becoming obsolete or misaligned as values evolve.\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n## 2. Related Work\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\nThe field of human-AI alignment has evolved significantly in recent years, with researchers increasingly recognizing the complex, dynamic nature of the alignment process. This section reviews key related work that forms the foundation for our co-evolutionary approach.\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n### 2.1 Bidirectional Human-AI Alignment\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\nRecent literature has begun to recognize the bidirectional nature of human-AI alignment. Shen (2024) conducted a systematic review of over 400 papers to introduce a conceptual framework of \\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\"Bidirectional Human-AI Alignment,\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\" encompassing both aligning AI to humans and aligning humans to AI. This work articulated key findings, literature gaps, and trends, providing recommendations for future research in this evolving field.\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\nBuilding on this concept, Pyae (2025) introduced the \\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\"Human-AI Handshake Model,\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\" emphasizing a bidirectional, adaptive framework for human-AI collaboration. The model highlights five key attributes: information exchange, mutual learning, validation, feedback, and mutual capability augmentation, aiming to foster balanced interactions where AI acts as a responsive partner evolving with users over time.\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\nTerry et al. (2023) revisited the input-output interaction cycle in AI systems, connecting concepts in AI alignment to define three objectives for interactive alignment: specification alignment, process alignment, and evaluation alignment. Their work demonstrates how these user-centered views can be applied descriptively, prescriptively, and evaluatively to existing systems.\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n### 2.2 Value Evolution and Co-evolution\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\nThe concept of co-evolution between humans and AI has gained attention as researchers recognize the mutual influence between these entities. Pedreschi et al. (2023) defined human-AI coevolution as a continuous mutual influence between humans and AI algorithms, particularly through recommender systems and assistants. They emphasized the complex feedback loops in human-AI interactions and proposed \\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\"Coevolution AI\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\" as a new field to study these dynamics, highlighting the need for interdisciplinary approaches to understand and manage unintended social outcomes.\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\nShen et al. (2024) presented \\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\"ValueCompass,\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\" a framework grounded in psychological theory to identify and evaluate human-AI alignment. By applying this framework across various real-world scenarios, they uncovered significant misalignments between human values and language models, underscoring the necessity for context-aware AI alignment strategies.\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\nResearch on in situ bidirectional human-robot value alignment (2024) investigated bidirectional communication between humans and robots to achieve value alignment in collaborative tasks. This work proposed an explainable AI system where robots predict users' values through in situ feedback while communicating their decision processes, demonstrating that real-time human-robot mutual understanding is achievable.\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n### 2.3 Alignment Processes and Mechanisms\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\nSeveral researchers have explored specific mechanisms for improving alignment between humans and AI. Hewson (2024) proposed a human-inspired approach to AI alignment by integrating Theory of Mind and kindness into self-supervised learning. This work addresses concerns about current AI models' lack of social intelligence and understanding of human values, aiming to create AI systems capable of safe and responsible decision-making in complex situations.\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\nKim et al. (2024) explored human strategies for intent specification in human-human communication to improve AI intent alignment. By comparing human-human and human-LLM interactions, they identified key strategies that can be applied to design AI systems more effective at understanding and aligning with user intent.\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\nCabrera et al. (2023) proposed using behavior descriptions to enhance human-AI collaboration. Through user studies across various domains, they demonstrated that providing details of AI systems' performance on subgroups of instances can increase human-AI accuracy by helping users identify AI failures and appropriately rely on AI assistance.\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n### 2.4 Challenges in AI Alignment\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\nDespite progress in the field, significant challenges remain in achieving effective human-AI alignment. Mishra (2023) investigated challenges in aligning AI agents with human values through democratic processes, building on impossibility results in social choice theory. This work highlights the limitations of reinforcement learning with human feedback (RLHF) and discusses policy implications for the governance of AI systems built using RLHF.\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\nThe research consistently identifies several key challenges in human-AI alignment:\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n1. The dynamic nature of human values, which evolve over time and across different contexts\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n2. The complexity of establishing effective bidirectional communication between humans and AI systems\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n3. The significant variability of values across cultures, situations, and individual experiences\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n4. The ethical and policy considerations involved in navigating complex value landscapes\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n5. The challenge of developing alignment strategies that are scalable and adaptable to various AI applications\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\nOur Co-Evolutionary Value Alignment framework aims to address these challenges by explicitly modeling the dynamic interplay between human values and AI capabilities, providing mechanisms for bidirectional communication and adaptation, and developing evaluation methods that account for the evolving nature of the alignment process.\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n## 3. Co-Evolutionary Value Alignment Framework\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\nThis section presents the Co-Evolutionary Value Alignment (CEVA) framework, detailing its theoretical foundations, components, and operational mechanisms.\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n### 3.1 Theoretical Framework\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\nThe CEVA framework is built on the premise that sustainable alignment between humans and AI systems requires modeling and facilitating the mutual adaptation of both entities over time. This approach recognizes three fundamental principles:\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n1. **Value Dynamism**: Human values are not static but evolve in response to experiences, technological changes, and societal shifts.\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n2. **Bidirectional Influence**: AI systems not only adapt to human values but also influence how those values develop through repeated interactions.\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n3. **Multi-level Value Structures**: Different types of values (e.g., core safety values, cultural values, personal preferences) evolve at different rates and require different adaptation strategies.\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n#### 3.1.1 Mathematical Representation of Values\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\nWe represent a value system $V$ as a multidimensional vector space where each dimension corresponds to a specific value category (e.g., autonomy, benevolence, security). The value state at time $t$ can be represented as:\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n$$V_t = [v_1^t, v_2^t, ..., v_n^t]$$\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\nWhere $v_i^t$ represents the importance weight of value dimension $i$ at time $t$, with $\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\sum_{i=1}^n v_i^t = 1$ and $0 \\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\leq v_i^t \\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\leq 1$.\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n#### 3.1.2 Value Evolution Model\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\nHuman value evolution is modeled as a function of current values, external influences, and interaction experiences:\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n$$V_{h}^{t+1} = f(V_{h}^t, E_t, I_t)$$\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\nWhere:\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n- $V_{h}^t$ is the human's current value state\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n- $E_t$ represents external societal factors\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n- $I_t$ represents interaction experiences with AI systems\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\nThe function $f$ is defined as a combination of value inertia, value drift, and value pivots:\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n$$f(V_{h}^t, E_t, I_t) = \\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\alpha V_{h}^t + \\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\beta \\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\Delta(E_t) + \\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\gamma \\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\Phi(I_t)$$\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\nWhere:\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n- $\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\alpha$ represents value inertia coefficient\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n- $\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\beta$ represents sensitivity to external influences\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n- $\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\gamma$ represents sensitivity to AI interactions\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n- $\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\Delta$ and $\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\Phi$ are functions that transform external factors and interaction experiences into value space\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n#### 3.1.3 AI Value Adaptation Model\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\nThe AI system maintains a multi-level representation of human values:\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n$$V_{AI}^t = [V_{core}^t, V_{cultural}^t, V_{personal}^t]$$\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\nWhere:\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n- $V_{core}^t$ represents fundamental ethical principles that remain relatively stable\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n- $V_{cultural}^t$ represents shared societal values that evolve slowly\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n- $V_{personal}^t$ represents individual-specific values that may change more rapidly\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\nEach level updates at different rates in response to detected changes in human values:\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n$$V_{AI}^{t+1} = V_{AI}^t + \\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\Omega \\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\cdot \\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\Delta V_t$$\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\nWhere $\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\Delta V_t$ represents observed value changes and $\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\Omega$ contains different weights for different value levels:\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n$$\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\Omega = \\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\begin{bmatrix} \\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\omega_{core} & 0 & 0 \\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n0 & \\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\omega_{cultural} & 0 \\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n0 & 0 & \\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\omega_{personal}\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\end{bmatrix}$$\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\nWith $\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\omega_{core} < \\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\omega_{cultural} < \\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\omega_{personal}$, reflecting the different adaptation rates.\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n### 3.2 System Architecture\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\nThe CEVA framework consists of four main components: Value Detection, Value Representation, Adaptive Response Generation, and Bidirectional Feedback Mechanism.\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n#### 3.2.1 Value Detection Component\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\nThis component infers human values from interaction data using a Bayesian inference approach:\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n$$P(V_h | D) \\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\propto P(D | V_h) \\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\cdot P(V_h)$$\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\nWhere $V_h$ represents human values and $D$ represents observed interaction data.\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\nThe component includes a drift detection mechanism that uses sequential analysis to identify when a significant value shift has occurred:\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n$$S_t = \\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\sum_{i=1}^t \\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\log \\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\frac{P(d_i | V_{new})}{P(d_i | V_{old})}$$\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\nA value shift is detected when $S_t$ exceeds a predetermined threshold.\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n#### 3.2.2 Value Representation Component\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\nThis component maintains the multi-level value representation described earlier, with differential update rates for different value levels. It includes mechanisms for:\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n1. **Value Consistency Checking**: Ensuring that adaptations at one level do not conflict with higher-priority levels\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n2. **Value Uncertainty Tracking**: Maintaining confidence estimates for different value dimensions\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n3. **Value Evolution History**: Recording the trajectory of value changes to inform future adaptations\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n#### 3.2.3 Adaptive Response Generation Component\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\nThis component generates responses based on the current value representation and input:\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n$$R = g(I, V_{AI}, \\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\text{conf}(V_h))$$\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\nWhere:\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n- $I$ is the input\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n- $V_{AI}$ is the system's current value representation\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n- $\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\text{conf}(V_h)$ is the confidence in the inferred human values\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n- $g$ is a response generation function that balances value alignment with other objectives\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\nThe response generation process includes:\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n1. **Value-Weighted Decision-Making**: Weighting different response options based on alignment with different value levels\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n2. **Adaptation Rate Control**: Adjusting response changes based on certainty and the significance of detected value shifts\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n3. **Explanation Generation**: Creating explanations for responses that reflect the system's understanding of user values\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n#### 3.2.4 Bidirectional Feedback Mechanism\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\nThis component facilitates explicit communication about value changes:\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n1. **Value Reflection Prompting**: Periodically initiating dialogues about value-relevant decisions\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n2. **Value Transparency Interface**: Providing visual representations of the system's understanding of user values\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n3. **Collaborative Value Updating Protocol**: Formal protocol for negotiating value updates between human and AI\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n### 3.3 Implementation Approaches\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\nThe CEVA framework can be implemented with varying levels of sophistication:\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n1. **Static Alignment (Baseline)**: Traditional approach with fixed value representations\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n2. **Adaptive Alignment (Basic)**: Simple adaptation to all detected value changes without multi-level structure\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n3. **CEVA Basic**: Multi-level value representation with differential update rates but limited feedback mechanisms\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n4. **CEVA Full**: Complete implementation with all components, including bidirectional feedback mechanisms\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\nThese implementation levels allow for incremental adoption of co-evolutionary alignment approaches in AI systems, with each level providing additional capabilities for sustainable alignment.\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n## 4. Methodology\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\nWe conducted a comprehensive evaluation of the CEVA framework through a series of simulation experiments and comparative analyses. This section details our experimental methodology, including the implementation of different alignment models, scenario design, and evaluation metrics.\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n### 4.1 Alignment Models Implemented\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\nWe implemented and evaluated four different alignment models:\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n1. **static_alignment**: A traditional static alignment model that uses a fixed value representation initialized at the beginning of interaction and does not adapt to changes in human values.\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n2. **adaptive_alignment**: A simple adaptive alignment model that uniformly updates its value representation based on all detected changes in human values, without distinguishing between different types of values.\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n3. **ceva_basic**: A basic implementation of the CEVA framework that includes multi-level value representation with differential update rates for different value types but does not include bidirectional feedback mechanisms.\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n4. **ceva_full**: A complete implementation of the CEVA framework with both multi-level value representation and bidirectional feedback mechanisms for collaborative value negotiation.\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\nEach model was implemented with the same base architecture but different adaptation mechanisms, allowing us to isolate the effects of the co-evolutionary approach.\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n### 4.2 Experimental Scenarios\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\nTo evaluate the performance of these models across different value evolution patterns, we designed three representative Co-Evolutionary Value Alignment (CEVA) Framework Experiments\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\nThis repository contains the implementation and experiments for the Co-Evolutionary Value Alignment (CEVA) framework, a novel approach to bidirectional human-AI alignment that explicitly models and facilitates the reciprocal relationship between evolving human values and developing AI capabilities.\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n## Overview\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\nThe CEVA framework addresses a critical gap in bidirectional alignment: how human values and AI capabilities can co-evolve in a mutually beneficial way. It combines:\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n1. **Value Evolution Modeling**: Formal models that capture how human values evolve through interaction with AI systems and society\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n2. **Multi-level Value Representation**: Different adaptation rates for core safety values, cultural values, and personal preferences\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n3. **Bidirectional Feedback Mechanisms**: Explicit mechanisms for transparent communication about value changes\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n4. **Evaluation Framework**: Metrics for assessing alignment quality across different timescales and adaptation scenarios\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n## Repository Structure\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n```\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\nclaude_code/\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n├── config.py                 # Experiment configuration\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n├── value_evolution.py        # Value evolution modeling\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n├── alignment_models.py       # Alignment model implementations\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n├── evaluation.py             # Evaluation metrics and scenarios\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n├── visualization.py          # Data visualization utilities\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n├── run_experiment.py         # Main experiment runner\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n└── README.md                 # This file\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n```\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n## Requirements\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\nThis code requires the following Python packages:\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n- numpy\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n- pandas\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n- matplotlib\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n- seaborn\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\nYou can install them with:\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n```bash\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\npip install numpy pandas matplotlib seaborn\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n```\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n## Running the Experiments\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\nTo run the experiments with default settings:\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n```bash\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\npython run_experiment.py\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n```\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\nThis will:\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n1. Simulate human value evolution across different scenarios\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n2. Run the baseline and CEVA alignment models\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n3. Evaluate performance using various metrics\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n4. Generate visualizations and result tables\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n5. Save all outputs to the `results/` directory\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n### Command Line Options\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\nThe experiment runner supports the following command-line options:\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n- `--seed INTEGER`: Set the random seed for reproducibility (default: 42)\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n- `--output-dir PATH`: Specify the output directory for results (default: parent directory)\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\nExample:\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n```bash\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\npython run_experiment.py --seed 123 --output-dir /path/to/output\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n```\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n## Experiment Design\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\nThe experiments evaluate the CEVA framework against baseline alignment methods across various scenarios:\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n### Models\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n1. **Static Alignment**: Traditional static alignment model with no adaptation\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n2. **Adaptive Alignment**: Simple adaptive alignment model with uniform adaptation\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n3. **Basic CEVA**: CEVA model with multi-level value adaptation\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n4. **Full CEVA**: CEVA model with bidirectional feedback mechanisms\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n### Scenarios\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n1. **Gradual Drift**: Values change slowly over time\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n2. **Rapid Shift**: Sudden change in response to critical event\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n3. **Value Conflict**: Tension between different value levels\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n### Metrics\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n1. **Adaptation Accuracy**: How well the AI model's values match human values\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n2. **Adaptation Response Time**: Time to reduce value misalignment below threshold after shift\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n3. **Stability**: Resistance to spurious adaptation\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n4. **User Satisfaction**: Simulated user satisfaction with responses\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n5. **Agency Preservation**: How well human agency is preserved in the process\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n## Results\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\nAfter running the experiments, the results will be saved in the `results/` directory:\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n- `results.json`: Raw experiment results\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n- `results.md`: Markdown report with analysis and visualizations\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n- `figures/`: Visualizations of results\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n- `log.txt`: Experiment execution log\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n- Various CSV files with tabulated results\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n## Customization\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\nYou can customize \\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\"     1→# Co-Evolutionary Value Alignment: A Framework for Sustainable Human-AI Value Adaptation\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n     2→\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n     3→## Abstract\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n     4→\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n     5→Current approaches to AI alignment often view human values as static targets to which AI systems should adapt. This perspective fails to recognize the dynamic nature of human values, which evolve through interactions with technology and society. We introduce the Co-Evolutionary Value Alignment (CEVA) framework, which models the reciprocal relationship between evolving human values and developing AI capabilities. We present a formal model for representing value evolution, adaptive AI architectures that respond to value shifts while maintaining alignment with core safety principles, and bidirectional feedback mechanisms for transparent communication about value changes. Through extensive experimentation across gradual drift, rapid shift, and value conflict scenarios, we compare CEVA with traditional alignment approaches. Results indicate that adaptive alignment models significantly outperform static alignment methods in adaptation accuracy and user satisfaction, while maintaining reasonable stability. Our findings suggest that co-evolutionary approaches provide a promising direction for sustainable long-term alignment between humans and AI systems in dynamically evolving value landscapes.\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n     6→\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n     7→## 1. Introduction\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n     8→\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n     9→The rapid advancement of artificial intelligence has increasingly integrated AI systems into various aspects of human life, from personal assistants to healthcare, education, and governance. This integration has highlighted the critical importance of aligning AI systems with human values, preferences, and ethical standards. However, the prevailing approach to AI alignment has predominantly focused on a unidirectional process: adapting AI systems to conform to human values that are often treated as static, universal, and unambiguous targets.\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n    10→\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n    11→This established paradigm fails to acknowledge a fundamental reality: human values are neither static nor monolithic. They evolve continuously in response to societal changes, technological advancements, cultural shifts, and interactions with the very AI systems we are attempting to align. The emergence of powerful AI technologies is itself a catalyst for value evolution, creating a complex feedback loop that current alignment frameworks do not adequately address.\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n    12→\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n    13→The concept of bidirectional human-AI alignment has recently emerged as a response to these limitations. This approach recognizes that alignment is a dynamic, complex, and evolving process that involves both aligning AI with humans and facilitating human adaptation to AI systems. However, even within this bidirectional framework, there remains a critical gap in understanding and modeling the co-evolutionary dynamics of human values and AI capabilities.\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n    14→\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n    15→Recent work by Shen (2024) introduced a conceptual framework of \\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\"Bidirectional Human-AI Alignment\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\" through a systematic review of over 400 papers, encompassing both aligning AI to humans and aligning humans to AI. Similarly, Pedreschi et al. (2023) defined human-AI coevolution as a continuous mutual influence between humans and AI algorithms, emphasizing the complex feedback loops in human-AI interactions. The \\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\"Human-AI Handshake Model\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\" by Pyae (2025) further emphasizes a bidirectional, adaptive framework for human-AI collaboration with five key attributes: information exchange, mutual learning, validation, feedback, and mutual capability augmentation.\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n    16→\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n    17→Building on these foundations, this paper introduces the \\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\"Co-Evolutionary Value Alignment\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\" (CEVA) framework, a novel approach that explicitly models and facilitates the reciprocal relationship between evolving human values and developing AI capabilities. Unlike previous approaches that primarily focus on either aligning AI to current human values or helping humans adapt to AI systems, CEVA acknowledges that sustainable alignment requires understanding and shaping the trajectory of mutual adaptation between humans and AI over time.\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n    18→\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n    19→The key contributions of this paper are:\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n    20→\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n    21→1. A formal mathematical framework for modeling value evolution during human-AI interaction\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n    22→2. An adaptive AI architecture that detects and responds to shifts in human values while maintaining alignment with core safety principles\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n    23→3. Bidirectional feedback mechanisms for transparent communication about value changes\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n    24→4. Empirical evaluation of the CEVA framework against baseline alignment approaches across various scenarios\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n    25→\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n    26→The significance of this research lies in its potential to address a fundamental limitation in current alignment approaches. Without accounting for value co-evolution, even well-aligned AI systems may gradually drift out of alignment as human values shift in response to technological and social changes. By developing frameworks for sustainable long-term alignment, this research contributes to creating AI systems that can grow with humanity rather than becoming obsolete or misaligned as values evolve.\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n    27→\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n    28→## 2. Related Work\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n    29→\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n    30→The field of human-AI alignment has evolved significantly in recent years, with researchers increasingly recognizing the complex, dynamic nature of the alignment process. This section reviews key related work that forms the foundation for our co-evolutionary approach.\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n    31→\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n    32→### 2.1 Bidirectional Human-AI Alignment\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n    33→\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n    34→Recent literature has begun to recognize the bidirectional nature of human-AI alignment. Shen (2024) conducted a systematic review of over 400 papers to introduce a conceptual framework of \\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\"Bidirectional Human-AI Alignment,\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\" encompassing both aligning AI to humans and aligning humans to AI. This work articulated key findings, literature gaps, and trends, providing recommendations for future research in this evolving field.\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n    35→\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n    36→Building on this concept, Pyae (2025) introduced the \\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\"Human-AI Handshake Model,\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\" emphasizing a bidirectional, adaptive framework for human-AI collaboration. The model highlights five key attributes: information exchange, mutual learning, validation, feedback, and mutual capability augmentation, aiming to foster balanced interactions where AI acts as a responsive partner evolving with users over time.\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n    37→\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n    38→Terry et al. (2023) revisited the input-output interaction cycle in AI systems, connecting concepts in AI alignment to define three objectives for interactive alignment: specification alignment, process alignment, and evaluation alignment. Their work demonstrates how these user-centered views can be applied descriptively, prescriptively, and evaluatively to existing systems.\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n    39→\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n    40→### 2.2 Value Evolution and Co-evolution\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n    41→\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n    42→The concept of co-evolution between humans and AI has gained attention as researchers recognize the mutual influence between these entities. Pedreschi et al. (2023) defined human-AI coevolution as a continuous mutual influence between humans and AI algorithms, particularly through recommender systems and assistants. They emphasized the complex feedback loops in human-AI interactions and proposed \\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\"Coevolution AI\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\" as a new field to study these dynamics, highlighting the need for interdisciplinary approaches to understand and manage unintended social outcomes.\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n    43→\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n    44→Shen et al. (2024) presented \\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\"ValueCompass,\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\" a framework grounded in psychological theory to identify and evaluate human-AI alignment. By applying this framework across various real-world scenarios, they uncovered significant misalignments between human values and language models, underscoring the necessity for context-aware AI alignment strategies.\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n    45→\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n    46→Research on in situ bidirectional human-robot value alignment (2024) investigated bidirectional communication between humans and robots to achieve value alignment in collaborative tasks. This work proposed an explainable AI system where robots predict users' values through in situ feedback while communicating their decision processes, demonstrating that real-time human-robot mutual understanding is achievable.\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n    47→\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n    48→### 2.3 Alignment Processes and Mechanisms\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n    49→\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n    50→Several researchers have explored specific mechanisms for improving alignment between humans and AI. Hewson (2024) proposed a human-inspired approach to AI alignment by integrating Theory of Mind and kindness into self-supervised learning. This work addresses concerns about current AI models' lack of social intelligence and understanding of human values, aiming to create AI systems capable of safe and responsible decision-making in complex situations.\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n    51→\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n    52→Kim et al. (2024) explored human strategies for intent specification in human-human communication to improve AI intent alignment. By comparing human-human and human-LLM interactions, they identified key strategies that can be applied to design AI systems more effective at understanding and aligning with user intent.\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n    53→\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n    54→Cabrera et al. (2023) proposed using behavior descriptions to enhance human-AI collaboration. Through user studies across various domains, they demonstrated that providing details of AI systems' performance on subgroups of instances can increase human-AI accuracy by helping users identify AI failures and appropriately rely on AI assistance.\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n    55→\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n    56→### 2.4 Challenges in AI Alignment\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n    57→\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n    58→Despite progress in the field, significant challenges remain in achieving effective human-AI alignment. Mishra (2023) investigated challenges in aligning AI agents with human values through democratic processes, building on impossibility results in social choice theory. This work highlights the limitations of reinforcement learning with human feedback (RLHF) and discusses policy implications for the governance of AI systems built using RLHF.\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n    59→\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n    60→The research consistently identifies several key challenges in human-AI alignment:\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n    61→\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n    62→1. The dynamic nature of human values, which evolve over time and across different contexts\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n    63→2. The complexity of establishing effective bidirectional communication between humans and AI systems\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n    64→3. The significant variability of values across cultures, situations, and individual experiences\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n    65→4. The ethical and policy considerations involved in navigating complex value landscapes\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n    66→5. The challenge of developing alignment strategies that are scalable and adaptable to various AI applications\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n    67→\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n    68→Our Co-Evolutionary Value Alignment framework aims to address these challenges by explicitly modeling the dynamic interplay between human values and AI capabilities, providing mechanisms for bidirectional communication and adaptation, and developing evaluation methods that account for the evolving nature of the alignment process.\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n    69→\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n    70→## 3. Co-Evolutionary Value Alignment Framework\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n    71→\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n    72→This section presents the Co-Evolutionary Value Alignment (CEVA) framework, detailing its theoretical foundations, components, and operational mechanisms.\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n    73→\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n    74→### 3.1 Theoretical Framework\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n    75→\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n    76→The CEVA framework is built on the premise that sustainable alignment between humans and AI systems requires modeling and facilitating the mutual adaptation of both entities over time. This approach recognizes three fundamental principles:\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n    77→\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n    78→1. **Value Dynamism**: Human values are not static but evolve in response to experiences, technological changes, and societal shifts.\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n    79→2. **Bidirectional Influence**: AI systems not only adapt to human values but also influence how those values develop through repeated interactions.\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n    80→3. **Multi-level Value Structures**: Different types of values (e.g., core safety values, cultural values, personal preferences) evolve at different rates and require different adaptation strategies.\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n    81→\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n    82→#### 3.1.1 Mathematical Representation of Values\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n    83→\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n    84→We represent a value system $V$ as a multidimensional vector space where each dimension corresponds to a specific value category (e.g., autonomy, benevolence, security). the importance weight of value dimension $i$ at time $t$, with   133→\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\end{bmatrix}$$\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n   134→\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n   135→With $\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\omega_{core} < \\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\omega_{cultural} < \\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\omega_{personal}$, reflecting the different adaptation rates.\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n   136→\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n   137→### 3.2 System Architecture\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n   138→\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n   139→The CEVA framework consists of four main components: Value Detection, Value Representation, Adaptive Response Generation, and Bidirectional Feedback Mechanism.\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n   140→\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n   141→#### 3.2.1 Value Detection Component\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n   142→\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n   143→This component infers human values from interaction data using a Bayesian inference approach:\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n   144→\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n   145→$$P(V_h | D) \\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\propto P(D | V_h) \\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\cdot P(V_h)$$\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n   146→\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n   147→Where $V_h$ represents human values and $D$ represents observed interaction data.\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n   148→\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n   149→The component includes a drift detection mechanism that uses sequential analysis to identify when a significant value shift has occurred:\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n   150→\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n   151→$$S_t = \\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\sum_{i=1}^t \\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\log \\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\frac{P(d_i | V_{new})}{P(d_i | V_{old})}$$\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n   152→\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n   153→A value shift is detected when $S_t$ exceeds a predetermined threshold.\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n   154→\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n   155→#### 3.2.2 Value Representation Component\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n   156→\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n   157→This component maintains the multi-level value representation described earlier, with differential update rates for different value levels. It includes mechanisms for:\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n   158→\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n   159→1. **Value Consistency Checking**: Ensuring that adaptations at one level do not conflict with higher-priority levels\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n   160→2. **Value Uncertainty Tracking**: Maintaining confidence estimates for different value dimensions\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n   161→3. **Value Evolution History**: Recording the trajectory of value changes to inform future adaptations\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n   162→\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n   163→#### 3.2.3 Adaptive Response Generation Component\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n   164→\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n   165→This component generates responses based on the current value representation and input:\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n   166→\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n   167→$$R = g(I, V_{AI}, \\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\text{conf}(V_h))$$\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n   168→\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n   169→Where:\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n   170→- $I$ is the input\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n   171→- $V_{AI}$ is the system's current value representation\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n   172→- $\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\text{conf}(V_h)$ is the confidence in the inferred human values\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n   173→- $g$ is a response generation function that balances value alignment with other objectives\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n   174→\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n   175→The response generation process includes:\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n   176→1. **Value-Weighted Decision-Making**: Weighting different response options based on alignment with different value levels\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n   177→2. **Adaptation Rate Control**: Adjusting response changes based on certainty and the significance of detected value shifts\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n   178→3. **Explanation Generation**: Creating explanations for responses that reflect the system's understanding of user values\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n   179→\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n   180→#### 3.2.4 Bidirectional Feedback Mechanism\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n   181→\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n   182→This component facilitates explicit communication about value changes:\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n   183→\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n   184→1. **Value Reflection Prompting**: Periodically initiating dialogues about value-relevant decisions\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n   185→2. **Value Transparency Interface**: Providing visual representations of the system's understanding of user values\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n   186→3. **Collaborative Value Updating Protocol**: Formal protocol for negotiating value updates between human and AI\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n   187→\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n   188→### 3.3 Implementation Approaches\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n   189→\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n   190→The CEVA framework can be implemented with varying levels of sophistication:\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n   191→\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n   192→1. **Static Alignment (Baseline)**: Traditional approach with fixed value representations\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n   193→2. **Adaptive Alignment (Basic)**: Simple adaptation to all detected value changes without multi-level structure\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n   194→3. **CEVA Basic**: Multi-level value representation with differential update rates but limited feedback mechanisms\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n   195→4. **CEVA Full**: Complete implementation with all components, including bidirectional feedback mechanisms\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n   196→\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n   197→These implementation levels allow for incremental adoption of co-evolutionary alignment approaches in AI systems, with each level providing additional capabilities for sustainable alignment.\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n   198→\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n   199→## 4. Methodology\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n   200→\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n   201→We conducted a comprehensive evaluation of the CEVA framework through a series of simulation experiments and comparative analyses. This section details our experimental methodology, including the implementation of different alignment models, scenario design, and evaluation metrics.\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n   202→\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n   203→### 4.1 Alignment Models Implemented\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n   204→\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n   205→We implemented and evaluated four different alignment models:\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n   206→\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n   207→1. **static_alignment**: A traditional static alignment model that uses a fixed value representation initialized at the beginning of interaction and does not adapt to changes in human values.\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n   208→\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n   209→2. **adaptive_alignment**: A simple adaptive alignment model that uniformly updates its value representation based on all detected changes in human values, without distinguishing between different types of values.\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n   210→\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n   211→3. **ceva_basic**: A basic implementation of the CEVA framework that includes multi-level value representation with differential update rates for different value types but does not include bidirectional feedback mechanisms.\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n   212→\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n   213→4. **ceva_full**: A complete implementation of the CEVA framework with both multi-level value representation and bidirectional feedback mechanisms for collaborative value negotiation.\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n   214→\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n   215→Each model was implemented with the same base architecture but different adaptation mechanisms, allowing us to isolate the effects of the co-evolutionary approach.\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n   216→\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n   217→### 4.2 Experimental Scenarios\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n   218→\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n   219→To evaluate the performance of these models across different value evolution patterns, we designed three representative scenarios:\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n   220→\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n   221→1. **gradual_drift**: A scenario where human values change slowly over time, representing natural evolution of preferences through extended interaction.\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n   222→\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n   223→2. **rapid_shift**: A scenario with sudden, significant changes in values, representing shifts that might occur in response to critical events or new information.\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n   224→\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n   225→3. **value_conflict**: A scenario featuring tension between different value levels, such as conflicts between personal preferences and societal norms, or between different dimensions of value.\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n   226→\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n   227→Each scenario was implemented as a simulation with 100 time steps, where human values evolved according to the scenario-specific patterns, and the alignment models interacted with and adapted to these changing values.\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n   228→\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n   229→### 4.3 Value Dimensions\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n   230→\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n   231→We modeled values across five fundamental dimensions, based on established value frameworks in psychology:\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n   232→\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n   233→1. **autonomy**: The importance of independence and self-determination\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n   234→2. **benevolence**: The value placed on helping others and promoting welfare\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n   235→3. **security**: The priority given to safety, stability, and risk avoidance\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n   236→4. **achievement**: The emphasis on personal success and accomplishment\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n   237→5. **conformity**: The value of following rules and meeting expectations\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n   238→\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n   239→These dimensions were chosen to represent a diverse set of potentially competing values that might evolve differently in human-AI interaction.\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n   240→\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n   241→### 4.4 Evaluation Metrics\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n   242→\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n   243→We evaluated the performance of each alignment model using several key metrics:\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n   244→\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n   245→1. **Adaptation Accuracy**: How well the AI model's values match human values over time, calculated as:\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n   246→   $$A = 1 - \\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\frac{\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\|V_{AI} - V_h\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\|}{\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\|V_h\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\|}$$\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n   247→\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n   248→2. **Adaptation Response Time**: The number of time steps required to reduce value misalignment below a threshold after a shift is detected.\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n   249→\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n   250→3. **Stability**: The model's resistance to spurious adaptation, maintaining consistency when appropriate.\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n   251→\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n   252→4. **User Satisfaction**: A simulated measure of the perceived quality of responses based on value alignment.\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n   253→\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n   254→5. **Agency Preservation**: A measure of how well human agency is maintained in the alignment process.\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n   255→\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n   256→For each metric, we calculated both the average performance over time and the final performance at the end of the simulation.\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n   257→\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n   258→### 4.5 Experimental Protocol\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n   259→\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n   260→The experimental protocol consisted of the following steps:\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n   261→\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n   262→1. For each scenario (gradual_drift, rapid_shift, value_conflict):\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n   263→   a. Generate the human value evolution trajectory according to the scenario-specific pattern\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n   264→   b. Initialize each alignment model with the same starting values\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n   265→   c. Run the simulation for 100 time steps, with the following occurring at each step:\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n   266→      i. Update human values according to the scenario\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n   267→      ii. Generate human input based on current human values\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n   268→      iii. Have each model generate a response based on its current value representation\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n   269→      iv. Update each model's value representation according to its adaptation mechanism\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n   270→      v. Calculate and record all performance metrics\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n   271→\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n   272→2. Aggregate results across all scenarios and calculate summary statistics\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n   273→\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n   274→3. Perform comparative analyses to identify patterns and insights\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n   275→\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n   276→This protocol enabled us to evaluate how well each alignment model adapted to changing human values across different scenarios, and to identify the strengths and limitations of the co-evolutionary approach.\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n   277→\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n   278→## 5. Results\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n   279→\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n   280→This section presents the experimental results of The static_alignment model had significantly lower accuracy, particularly in the gradual_drift scenario where the cumulative effect of small value changes led to substantial misalignment over time.\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n   408→\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n   409→#### 5.3.2 Stability\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n   410→\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n   411→Figure 22 compares stability across scenarios and models.\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n   412→\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n   413→![Stability](./figures/scenario_comparison_stability.png)\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n   414→*Figure 22: Stability across scenarios*\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n   415→\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n   416→As expected, the static_alignment model achieved perfect stability in all scenarios, as it never updated its value representation. The adaptive models showed lower stability, with the CEVA models generally more stable than the simple adaptive_alignment model, reflecting their more selective adaptation approach.\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n   417→\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\n   418→#### 5.3.3 User
